note: An intermediate guitar plus theory and ear week at 30 minutes a day: 7th chords and the ii-V-I are heard, named, played as shapes, arpeggios and guide tones, moved to a new key and improvised over, with an ear or theory exercise every day between the guitar work.

plan.title: Week 1: 7th chords and the ii-V-I
plan.summary: Hear and name 7th chords, then play the ii-V-I as shapes, arpeggios, guide tones and solos in C and G, with the relative minor and a blues for contrast.

exercises.title: Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 shapes
exercises.focus: Open ii-V-I shapes in C · slow changes

sections.text: These three shapes are the ii-V-I in C, the most common chord move in jazz and many ballads.
Strum each shape and pick each string to check it. Then Dm7 to G7 to Cmaj7, four strums each, slowly, ten times round.

exercises.title: Name the chord
exercises.focus: Major, minor, 7, maj7, m7 by ear

sections.text: Naming a chord's quality by ear is the skill behind working out songs.
Name each chord you hear. Listen to the top note: a half step under the octave is maj7, a whole step is 7 or m7. Count how many of twenty you get.

exercises.title: Arpeggios of the ii-V-I
exercises.focus: Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 arpeggios, one box each

sections.text: An arpeggio is the chord one note at a time, so a solo built from it outlines the changes.
Dm7
Play the Dm7 arpeggio up and down at 70, one note per click: {{1}} {{b3}} {{5}} {{b7}}.
G7
G7: {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} {{b7}}. Its {{3}} (B) and {{b7}} (F) are a tritone apart, the tension that wants to resolve.
Cmaj7
Cmaj7: {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} {{7}}. Then all three in a row, one bar each, without stopping.
Comping means playing the chords in rhythm under a melody; short, light strums leave room for it.
Two strums a bar
Press Play and strum short chords on beats 2 and 4, one bar each of Dm7, G7, Cmaj7, Cmaj7.
Bass and chord
Now pick each chord's root on beats 1 and 3 and strum the top strings on 2 and 4, like the backing.

exercises.title: Alternate picking
exercises.focus: Down-up, three notes per string, 90 bpm

sections.text: Three notes per string puts the pick on alternating strokes at each string crossing.
Three notes per string, down-up, across all six and back at 90.

exercises.title: ii, V and I in the scale

sections.text: Stack 3rds on each note of C major and the chords on {{2}}, {{5}} and {{1}} are Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7.
Build them
Tap {{2}} {{4}} {{6}} {{1}} on the staff: Dm7, every other note from D. Then {{5}} {{7}} {{2}} {{4}}: G7. Then {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} {{7}}: Cmaj7.
Hear the pull
Press Play and listen: ii moves away, V leans hard, I lands. Say each numeral as it arrives.
The 3rd and 7th of each chord move by a half step or not at all, so they make the changes audible with two notes.
The 3rd-7th line
Press Play and play the notes shown, one per beat: F over Dm7 (its 3rd), F over G7 (its 7th), E over Cmaj7 (its 3rd).
The 7th-3rd line
Now the other line: C over Dm7 (its 7th), B over G7 (its 3rd), B over Cmaj7 (its 7th). Then alternate the two lines.
Starting each chord on a guide tone is the quickest way to make a solo follow the changes.
Land on the targets
Press Play and improvise in C major, landing on a lit target as each chord arrives.
Fewer notes
Same backing; now only three or four notes per chord, always including its guide tone.

exercises.title: Legato warm-up
exercises.focus: Legato trill · fingers 1-3 · G string, 5th fret

sections.text: Hammer-ons and pull-offs build left-hand strength without the pick.
Pick once, then hammer finger 3 and pull to finger 1 evenly on the click, 30 seconds on, 15 off, three rounds at 80.

exercises.title: C major and A minor, same notes
exercises.focus: C major → A natural minor over one click

sections.text: A minor uses exactly the notes of C major; only the home note changes, and with it the mood.
Hear the home move
Press Play: four bars of C major over C, then four of A minor over Am. The notes are the same; listen to where each one comes to rest.
La is home
Tap {{1}} (A) on the staff, then walk up to the C above it: in C major that C is Do, here it is the {{b3}}. A minor is C major starting from La.

exercises.title: One shape, two keys
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic box 1 = C major pentatonic

sections.text: The relative minor works on the neck too: one pentatonic box serves both keys, with a different root.
As A minor
Play box 1 at the 5th fret up and down at 80, starting and ending on {{1}} (A).
As C major
The same frets, but now the home is {{1}} (C): start and end there, and the box sounds bright.

exercises.title: Major or minor song?
exercises.focus: C-G-Am-F vs Am-F-C-G by ear and by hand

sections.text: The same four chords can sound major or minor depending on which one feels like home.
Start on C
Press Play and strum along: C, G, Am, F. Notice C feels like home.
Start on Am
Now Am, F, C, G: the same chords, but Am is home and it sounds minor. Strum along, then stop and say which chord feels finished.
The same move in a new key: Am7 is ii, D7 is V, Gmaj7 is I in G.
Strum each shape and check each string. Then Am7 to D7 to Gmaj7, four strums each, ten times round.
The 7th is what separates D7 from Gmaj7; hearing it alone makes the chords easy to name.
Name each interval: a minor 7th (as in D7) or a major 7th (as in Gmaj7). Done at ten right in a row.
Moving the arpeggios to G shows they are shapes of degrees, not lists of frets.
Am7 and D7
Play the Am7 arpeggio up and down at 70: {{1}} {{b3}} {{5}} {{b7}}.
Gmaj7, then all three
Gmaj7: {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} {{7}}. Then all three arpeggios in a row, one bar each, at 70.
Guide tones in a new key: C to C to B, or G to F♯ to F♯.
Guide tones only
Press Play and play only the targets, one long note per chord, choosing either line.
Fill in around them
Same backing; now improvise in G major, still landing on a target at each change. Record the last two minutes.
Arpeggios jump strings, so the pick hand needs to jump accurately.
Two notes per string, down-up, skipping a string each time, at 80.
Answering quickly makes chord hearing work at song speed.
Name each chord as fast as you can for 30 seconds, then rest. Four rounds; beat your day 1 score.
I-vi-ii-V adds the vi to the ii-V-I, and it is the loop under countless songs.
With the chart
Press Play and say each numeral as it arrives: I (Cmaj7), vi (Am7), ii (Dm7), V (G7).
In a new order
Now a different order of the same four. Look away, write down the numerals you hear for one pass, then check.
Playing one loop with different comping feels is how a rhythm part stays interesting.
Block chords on 2 and 4
Press Play and strum short chords on beats 2 and 4.
Bass and chord
Root on 1 and 3, chord on 2 and 4.
Arpeggiated
Pick each chord low to high in eighth notes, letting the notes ring.

exercises.title: Legato, fingers 2-4
exercises.focus: Legato trill · fingers 2-4 · B string, 7th fret

sections.text: The weaker finger pair needs the most work.
Pick once, then hammer finger 4 and pull to finger 2 on the click, 30 seconds on, 15 off, three rounds at 70.

exercises.title: Why blues uses three 7ths
exercises.focus: A7, D7, E7 as I7, IV7, V7

sections.text: Blues breaks the rule of one dominant per key: every chord is a 7th, which gives the style its restless sound.
The three chords
A7, D7 and E7 are built on {{1}}, {{4}} and {{5}} of A. Tap each shape and hear the same dominant colour three times.
A7's own notes
Tap the A7 arpeggio: {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} {{b7}}. Its {{3}} is C♯, which is not in A minor pentatonic; that clash is the blues.

exercises.title: Twelve-bar in A
exercises.focus: 12-bar blues with A7, D7, E7 at 90 bpm

sections.text: The twelve-bar form is a fixed road map: learn it once and you can join any blues jam.
Follow the form
Press Play and strum along: four bars A7, two D7, two A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Count the bars out loud.
Without counting
Same form with a bass-and-chord feel. Keep going without counting aloud; done at two choruses with no wrong change.

exercises.title: Solo with the 3rd
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic + C♯ over A7-D7

sections.text: Adding the chord's 3rd to the pentatonic box makes a blues solo follow the changes.
Slide into C♯
Improvise in box 1. Over A7, slide from {{b3}} (C) up to {{c-sharp}}: not in A minor pentatonic, but the 3rd of A7, so it sounds like the chord. Land on {{1}} to finish phrases.
Over D7
Same backing; over D7 aim at {{d}}, and over A7 keep sliding into {{c-sharp}}.

days.theme: Review: the week in one jam

exercises.title: ii-V-I shapes in C and G

sections.text: Both keys back to back shows the shapes are under your fingers.
Four strums per chord: the ii-V-I in C twice, then in G twice, without stopping between keys.
The week's ear work as a score to beat next week.
Twenty chords; write down your score and compare it with days 1 and 5.
Playing them without help is the test that the shapes are yours.
Without looking
Press Play and play each arpeggio from memory as its chord comes round: root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, one per beat.
Check and fix
Switch to the neck view and check every note; replay any chord you missed until it is clean at 80.

exercises.title: ii-V-I jam
exercises.focus: Guide tones, then free soloing over Dm7-G7-Cmaj7

sections.text: Guide tones, arpeggios and the scale together are what make a solo over changes sound sure.
Guide tones
Press Play. Play one guide tone per chord, either line from day 2.
Arpeggio phrases
Same backing; start each chord with a run up its arpeggio, then leave space.
Free, and record
Improvise freely, still landing on a target at each change. Record it and keep it for next week.
